## TL;DR

I used the macOS Hub after the sidebar-color fix, then followed the review findings through five engineering rounds. The Hub now keeps startup reachability separate from saved server data, persists trusted identity learned from successful loopback health checks, and retains the local project path needed to manage a server after it goes offline. The final follow-up exposed an additional serialization defect: `ServerEntry` decoded `repositoryName` but omitted it from its custom encoder. That field is now encoded. A regression test verifies startup discovery, edit, and an offline reload still expose “Start local server,” without the startup sweep writing health or timestamp fields.

`xcodebuild` passed the macOS Hub tests. `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed on the third remote run: 123 changed test files, 2,136 tests passed with one skipped, the boot timing tests passed, and the UI smoke and rendered contrast gates passed. The first two remote runs were not green: one exposed a runner-only contrast mismatch that did not reproduce locally, and another hit a known timing-sensitive assertion in `agent-review.test.ts`. The third run completed successfully without a source change between check attempts.

## Work and rationale

The QA pass uncovered that a successful startup health sweep had been updating and saving server health for every saved server. This violated the requirement to leave Nick’s Hub registry untouched. Health results and check timestamps are now held in a volatile map. Later unrelated saves therefore cannot flush them into `servers.json`. Attention coordination receives the volatile health view so offline servers stop contributing to badges, while the saved registry remains unchanged for health fields.

I fixed the status lifecycle around WebKit load failures as well. Connectivity failures now trigger a health refresh, so an offline overlay’s Retry updates the server’s reachability state, rather than only reloading the web view. Non-connectivity load failures such as blocked navigation and HTTP status do not incorrectly mark a live server offline. Cross-server search keeps the current query when server health changes and clears stale remote results when the palette is dismissed. Attention badges and Dock counts exclude unhealthy servers.

The final review identified an identity durability gap. The startup sweep must preserve only identity that the server actually reported: display name, repository name, and local project path. I added an identity-only write when those values change; health, `lastHealthAt`, and `updatedAt` remain outside that write. The editor path also needed to leave a learned local path in the persisted document before discarding its volatile overlay. During verification, the new test showed `repositoryName` remained nil after reload, leading me to find and fix the missing encoder field in `ServerEntry`.

The regression test seeds an address-derived loopback server, runs a startup health check that learns “RepoOS” and a project path, and checks the saved health and timestamps remain unchanged. It edits the entry, constructs a fresh state against the same registry with an offline checker, then asserts that local service management remains enabled and the Start action is present.

Other concrete QA fixes in this work include making the local serve banner accurately reflect its effective bind address, documenting `REPOOS_HUB_SUPPORT_DIRECTORY` for isolated QA runs, and tightening sidebar origin display. The QA report and screenshot references recorded each checked area; captures were app-window-only as required by the task.

## Approaches tried

I first kept startup health in a volatile overlay so later route visits, accent updates, edits, or reorder operations could not persist stale reachability. Review testing correctly caught that identity had been placed in the same overlay and would consequently be lost on edit or relaunch. I chose to persist identity fields as soon as a successful loopback check learns them, rather than copying health snapshots into `ServerRegistryDocument` during arbitrary saves. This keeps the disk and memory responsibilities explicit and ensures the local service menu can be reconstructed offline.

I validated the path at several layers: the macOS test uses a temporary registry directory, asserts the disk representation immediately after the startup sweep, performs an edit, then reloads and checks the resulting action model. This avoids using the real Hub support directory and tests the user-visible state rather than only testing the helper that copies values.

## Challenges and blockers

The first remote check failed its contrast audit on many Settings text pairs in the `clear-light` scope. A direct local run on the same tree passed all 16 theme scopes and 14 screen states. A later remote pass also passed the rendered contrast audit, so I treated the initial result as a runner rendering mismatch rather than changing unrelated UI colors. The second remote check hit `agent-review.test.ts` with an expected 409/received 400 assertion; this test had also shown timing sensitivity in prior runs. A third full scoped run passed all required gates.

The local Xcode installation emitted CoreDevice/CoreSimulator compatibility warnings, but they did not prevent the macOS test target from building and running. No additional blocker remains for this engineering handoff.

## Key learnings

Volatile operational state and durable identity are related at runtime but must not share persistence semantics. Overlaying a whole server entry is convenient for display, yet every later persistence path must either preserve intended durable fields or explicitly exclude ephemeral ones. Tests should include a subsequent save and a fresh reload, since an initial “did not save” assertion alone cannot detect a later unrelated write leaking volatile state.

Custom `Codable` implementations require symmetry checks for every durable property. `repositoryName` already had a coding key and decoder, which made the omission in `encode(to:)` easy to overlook; the restart regression test exposed it. Finally, local and remote browser audits can differ when a runner’s rendered theme state is unstable. Reproduction on both environments helped distinguish an environment-only result from a source change requirement.
